title: How to Test a Sticky Add-to-Cart Bar Without Hurting Desktop
excerpt: A sticky bar fixes a real mobile problem and can create a new one on desktop. Test it against revenue per visitor, not just add-to-cart clicks.
body: A sticky add to cart bar solves a genuine mobile problem, because the buy button scrolls out of view exactly when a shopper is deciding. It also creates a new one, since a bar covering the price, the variant selector, or the shipping estimate can push conversion the other way. The useful question is not whether sticky bars work in general. It is whether yours helps the specific page it sits on, and whether it helps the mobile visitors it was meant for.

Capture the baseline before you change anything. Record add to cart rate, checkout starts, and revenue per visitor separately for mobile and desktop across a couple of weeks. Without that split you cannot tell whether a result came from the change or from desktop traffic masking a mobile regression. Product pages behave very differently by device, and averaging them together is the most common reason a test on this element comes back inconclusive and gets abandoned.

Design the test around the trade off instead of around the feature. Keep the bar clear of variant selection, let it collapse when the shopper scrolls back to the top, and make sure the full price and shipping estimate remain visible on screen at all times. Then change one thing at a time: presence of the bar first, then trigger timing, then button wording. Bundling all three into one release means a positive result teaches you nothing you can reuse on the next template.

Watch quality metrics alongside the headline number. A sticky bar frequently lifts add to cart clicks while checkout completion stays flat or falls, because it makes adding easy but leaves the commitment unclear. Measure revenue per visitor and the ratio of cart additions to completed purchases. If additions climb while revenue per visitor does not move, the bar is generating intent it cannot convert, which usually points to missing shipping or returns detail rather than to a poorly designed button.

Set the stop rule before you launch the test. Decide the minimum sample size and the shortest run time, ideally two full weeks so weekday and weekend behavior both count, and promise yourself you will not call a result on day three because the number looks exciting. Early stopping on a low traffic store produces wins that evaporate. If you lack the traffic for a clean read, either pool results across all product pages using one shared bar, or skip the test and ship the safer variant.

Roll out by template rather than site wide. What works on a single product page with one image and three variants may behave differently on a bundle page with a long description and multiple options. Keep a short log of what you tested, where, and what happened, so the next round starts from evidence instead of opinion.
